facts.text: Yosemite Valley, whose Miwok name means “killer,” is a 7.5‑mile long glacial valley surrounded by granite giants like Half Dome and El Capitan.
Yosemite Falls, the tallest waterfall in North America, pours over 2,400 feet of vertical drop, especially dramatic in spring meltwater.
The 1849 Gold Rush sparked violent clashes between miners and Native Americans, prompting the state to send the Mariposa Battalion to the Yosemite area.
In the 1870s, landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted and clergyman Thomas Starr King lobbied Senator John Conness to protect Yosemite, leading to its first national park status.
Camp 4, a historic climbing camp on the north side of El Capitan, became the birthplace of modern rock climbing after World War II.
Yosemite’s early history is marked by three cultural phases—Crane Flat, Tarmarack, and Mariposa—each reflecting shifts in hunting and tool use before European contact.
